title: Two switching implications proved; 23 sufficient failure classes remain
body:
The new case analysis follows the proposal to assume an overlap and study another opening. Moving the opening repairs all three old local pairs. For opposite petals, the two route-angle sums add to 360° plus the deficit at w, so under the sharpest-apex hypothesis the same petals cannot overlap along both routes.

Reusing the conditional hinge reduction gives 24 sufficient classes from the original 49. This removes redundant obligations. The angle identity then excludes original class 49, leaving 23 open. The complete rule and octahedron theorem remain unproved; the earlier notes are retained below.

title: Four opening positions; 49 simultaneous-failure classes to study
body:
The new octahedron proposal keeps the sharpest apex but allows four positions for the opening at the opposite vertex. An exhaustive combinatorial enumeration reduces simultaneous failure to 49 symmetry classes; none of these new geometric classes is yet excluded.

A comparison on 3,000 sampled shapes found a successful choice throughout. This is numerical evidence only. The earlier single-choice proof still has two gaps, and the seven excluded minus-edge classes remain recorded below.

title: Seven universal failure classes excluded; 21 remain
body:
The new proof step applies Pinciu’s face-neighborhood theorem to one previously residual pair in each tree. It excludes seven of the original 28 simultaneous-failure classes throughout the full convex realization space.

The remaining 21 classes and two-tree conjecture are open. The coordinate-box certificate is unchanged. Targeted numerical searches and exact checks of eight near-flat candidates did not close further classes.

title: Two candidate trees; one now certifies the entire old box
body:
The new two-choice rule switches between two off-quadrilateral stars. Each net consists of two vertex fans. It survived 23,000 discovery shapes and a separate 10,000-shape holdout; its universal validity remains conjectural.

Exact simplification: one of the two trees now covers the whole previously certified ±0.05 box, with 16 closed cells and 336 face-pair checks. The earlier proof used 409 cells and nine trees. The domain has not changed.

Exact examples show that each of the two individual trees can fail, and that all four quadrilateral-only routes can fail together. There is now an exhaustive target of 28 symmetry classes of simultaneous failure; no whole geometric class has yet been excluded. Numerical tests are not proofs.

title: Counts now distinguish proof gaps, local extent, and search coverage
body:
The new dashboard records 4 of 7 types proved, 2 of 3 opposite-petal angle branches proved, and the two remaining octahedron proof obligations. The 19 directly settled face pairs are separated from the four conditional ones.

Minus-edge progress is shown as certified half-widths ±0.01 → ±0.05 in the same ten-coordinate box. The two prism boxes are identified separately: box A is fully certified; box B has only 437/4194304 of its parameter volume marked covered by the search, with full independent replay pending.

A retained before-and-after table makes explicit that the latest research hour closed no universal proof gap. Its exact counterexamples and neighborhood results remain useful, separately recorded progress.

title: Apex-entry failure extends to a certified neighborhood
body:
New exact region: the apex-entry example persists when all eleven free shape coordinates vary independently by ±0.001. Every polyhedron in this closed box satisfies the selection rules, has the apex inside Ω, and still has a certified nonoverlapping net.

This strengthens the counterexample to the individual-apex shortcut. It does not prove the remaining joint-petal claim or Lemma L. The snapshots below retain the earlier discoveries and the prism investigation.

title: Prism route choices narrowed; general theorem still open
body:
Exact negative results: both quadrilateral routes from one fixed degree-four apex can fail. Even at the sharper degree-four apex, the shorter route can fail while the longer one succeeds. The prism section explains these checks.

Numerical lead only: retaining both routes at the sharper degree-four apex survived 60,000 sampled shapes. This does not prove the selection rule. The full n=6 theorem, Lemma L, and the small-fan-angle opposite-petal branch remain open.

The earlier snapshot below records this session’s exact apex-entry counterexample, radial clearance, and axis-nonclosure certificate. The original cone proof and bounded-region certificates remain valid.

title: An individual apex can enter; distances and closure matter
body:
Exactly refuted shortcut: a convex six-vertex example satisfies both selection rules but lets one outer apex enter Ω. All 28 pairs of its net remain nonoverlapping. The full theorem and the joint-petal problem remain open.

New exact checks: the local angular counterexample has a certified radial distance factor of at least 1.217 on every shared direction. A separate five-interval certificate proves that a proposed intrinsic metric cannot close into the prescribed convex octahedron, despite passing all local checks.

The earlier cone proof and 409-region minus-edge cover remain valid. Work continues on distance-sensitive local separation and the joint behavior of the opposite petals.

title: Morning research results · retained snapshot
body:
The full n=6 case remains unproved here. Direct review found an exact counterexample to the DF entry of DiBiase’s displayed octahedron chart. A base-cone proof handles the large-angle and equality branches. Lemma L and the remaining fan-angle sum below π are open.

Independent replay verified a complete 443-region prism-with-one-diagonal certificate and a larger 409-region octahedron-minus-edge certificate. These cover their stated parameter boxes, not whole combinatorial types. A new exact example rules out angular separation around w as a complete proof of Lemma L. Shared-length constraints also ruled out an earlier angle-only candidate. Global coverage remains open.
